details:
**Zheng He's treasure voyages**
Seven large naval expeditions (1405–1433) across the Indian Ocean led by the Muslim eunuch admiral Zheng He, sponsored mainly by the Yongle Emperor. They reached Southeast Asia, India, the Persian Gulf (Strait of Hormuz), and the Swahili Coast of East Africa, using enormous "treasure ships" (junks), and are one of the most common clues for the Ming.

**Forbidden City**
The vast imperial palace complex in Beijing, built under the Yongle Emperor after he moved the capital there from Nanjing. It remained the seat of Chinese emperors through the following Qing dynasty.

**Battle of Lake Poyang**
A huge 1363 naval battle on China's largest freshwater lake in which Zhu Yuanzhang defeated his rival Chen Youliang, leader of a rival "Han" regime, partly by using fire ships. The victory cleared his path to founding the Ming.

**Hongwu Emperor (Zhu Yuanzhang)**
The founder of the Ming, a former peasant and Buddhist monk who rose as a commander in the Red Turban Rebellion and proclaimed the dynasty in 1368, driving out the Mongol Yuan. He ruled harshly, purged officials after the alleged plot of chancellor Hu Weiyong, abolished the chancellorship, and imposed the haijin sea bans.

**Tumu Crisis**
A 1449 disaster in which the Zhengtong Emperor (temple name Yingzong), urged on by his eunuch Wang Zhen, personally led an army against the Oirat Mongols under Esen Taishi and was captured at Tumu Fortress. It is one of the most frequent mid-question clues for the dynasty.

**Yongle Emperor**
The third Ming emperor, whose reign name means "perpetual happiness." He took the throne from his nephew, the Jianwen Emperor, in the Jingnan Campaign, moved the capital to Beijing, built the Forbidden City and the Porcelain Tower of Nanjing, and sponsored Zheng He's voyages.

**Red Turban Rebellion**
A mid-14th-century uprising against the Mongol Yuan dynasty, tied to millenarian White Lotus Buddhist movements. Zhu Yuanzhang rose to power as a Red Turban commander, and the Ming emerged from it.

**Ming porcelain (blue-and-white vases)**
The dynasty is famous for its blue-and-white porcelain, made especially at the kilns of Jingdezhen, with notable advances in the Xuande era. "Ming vases" are the standard giveaway in questions on the dynasty.

**Li Zicheng and the Chongzhen Emperor's suicide**
In 1644 the rebel leader Li Zicheng, the "Dashing King," captured Beijing and declared a short-lived Shun dynasty. The last Ming emperor, Chongzhen, hanged himself from a tree on Jingshan (Coal Hill) behind the Forbidden City.

**Wu Sangui and Shanhai Pass**
A Ming general who opened the Shanhai Pass of the Great Wall to the Manchus in 1644 so they could help him defeat Li Zicheng. The Manchus then took Beijing and founded the Qing dynasty, ending the Ming.

**Giraffe presented as a qilin**
During the Yongle reign, a giraffe brought back from East Africa (Malindi) by the treasure fleet was presented at court as a qilin, a mythical auspicious beast, and taken as a sign of the emperor's Mandate of Heaven.

**Embroidered Uniform Guard (Jinyiwei)**
A secret police force set up by the Hongwu Emperor to spy on and punish officials. Together with the eunuch-run Eastern Depot, it is a recurring clue for Ming court repression.

**Matteo Ricci**
An Italian Jesuit missionary who reached China in the late 16th century and was eventually allowed to live in Beijing under the Wanli Emperor. He introduced European science and maps and founded what became the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception in Beijing.

**Gavin Menzies' 1421**
A widely discredited pseudohistory book, "1421: The Year China Discovered the World," arguing that a Ming treasure fleet sailed around the globe. Menzies, a former British submarine officer, focused on the sixth of Zheng He's voyages.

**Wei Zhongxian**
A powerful eunuch of the late Ming who controlled the court under the Tianqi Emperor, commanded the secret police, and violently persecuted the Donglin faction of reformist Confucian scholars.

**Nurhaci and the Seven Grievances**
The Jurchen (Manchu) leader who unified the Jurchen tribes and in 1618 issued the Seven Grievances, a list of complaints against the Ming that served as a declaration of war. His successors founded the Qing, which replaced the Ming.
